The Treefish (Sebastes serriceps) is a viviparous scorpaenid found in rocky subtidal habitats along the coast of southern California and Baja California. Females release planktonic yolk-sac larvae following a gestation period that coincides with late winter upwelling conditions. Newly extruded larvae are exceptionally small, with each larva weighing just 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams] immediately after parturition; this mass is derived from an egg diameter of approximately 0.8 millimeters, a common ovum size among small-bodied rockfishes. These lecithotrophic larvae are non-feeding during the first several days post-release, subsisting entirely on endogenous yolk reserves until mouth opening and retinal differentiation permit the onset of exogenous feeding. The species attains an ultimate total length of 41 centimeters [Li = 41 centimeters] in wild populations, a value observed in the oldest and largest specimens collected during long-term trawl surveys. Males and females grow at similar rates until the onset of gonadal recrudescence, after which females tend to achieve slightly larger asymptotic sizes, a pattern consistent with the energetic demands of internal fertilization and larval brooding.

Reproductive maturation in Treefish begins relatively early in the species' life cycle. Field otolith analyses indicate that individuals reach the total length at puberty of 19 centimeters [Lp = 19 centimeters], a size that corresponds to roughly 47 percent of the ultimate length. At this length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 89 grams [Wwp = approximately 89 grams], a body mass that signals the transition from juvenile somatic growth to the initiation of vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis. Upon reaching puberty, both sexes exhibit gonadosomatic indices that fluctuate seasonally, with peak gonadal investment observed during autumn months. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) recorded at a water temperature of 15.1 °C [T = 15.1 °C] is 4% [GSI = 4%]. This modest allocation is typical of iteroparous Sebastes species that spread reproductive effort across multiple annual events.

As individuals continue to grow beyond puberty, they approach an ultimate wet weight of 963 grams [Wwi = 963 grams], a mass that is attained around the same time as the maximum total length. This asymptotic body mass was derived from length-weight regressions using the 41 centimeter ultimate length and a species-specific conditional factor. The mass at birth of 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams] stands in stark contrast to the 963 gram adult maximum, representing an extraordinary mass increase of over six orders of magnitude between larval extrusion and terminal size. Such an extreme growth trajectory is supported by a piscivorous diet that includes juvenile rockfishes, cephalopods, and crustaceans, all of which are abundant in the kelp forest and rocky reef environments the species inhabits. The rapid growth phase in the first two years of life is critical to reducing vulnerability to gape-limited predators such as lingcod and larger conspecifics, as well as to California sea lions.

Longevity records for Treefish are derived from tag-recapture studies and validated otolith age readings conducted at ambient coastal seawater temperatures of 15.1 °C [T = 15.1 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, the maximum lifespan is 25 years [am = 25 years], a duration that places Sebastes serriceps among the moderately long-lived members of the subgenus Pteropodus at a temperature of 15.1 °C [T = 15.1 °C]. This maximum lifespan of 25 years [am = 25 years] is associated with a relatively slow pace of life that includes delayed senescence and sustained reproductive output well into the third decade of life at a temperature of 15.1 °C [T = 15.1 °C]. In comparison to the closely related gopher rockfish (Sebastes carnatus), which attains a maximum age of approximately 30 years, the Treefish's 25 year [am = 25 year] lifespan is slightly shorter but still considerably longer than that of many temperate nearshore teleosts. at a temperature of 15.1 °C [T = 15.1 °C] The consistent temperature of 15.1 °C [T = 15.1 °C] that characterizes the species' preferred depth range of 10 to 40 meters is thought to modulate metabolic rate and thereby influence both growth rate and actuarial senescence patterns.

Comparative life-history analysis places Treefish at an intermediate position along the fast-slow continuum within the genus. Confirming the total length at puberty as 19 centimeters [Lp = 19 centimeters] and the ultimate total length as 41 centimeters [Li = 41 centimeters] reinforces the pattern of moderate size at maturation relative to asymptotic size. The wet weight at puberty of 89 grams [Wwp = 89 grams] and the ultimate wet weight of 963 grams [Wwi = 963 grams] yield a size at maturity ratio similar to that of the vermilion rockfish, though the latter achieves a substantially larger asymptotic mass.
